title: Forest garden: the root layer
subtitle: Perennial root crops that harvest underground in a forest garden system.
excerpt: The root layer in a forest garden consists of perennial root crops (Jerusalem artichoke, oca, skirret, and other tubers) planted in gaps where light levels are too low for most fruiting crops but where the soil under the canopy remains workable.
sourceNotes: Root layer framework from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Species selection from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). Placement principles from Agroforestry Research Trust species trials.

glossaryTerms.definition: In a forest garden, the underground dimension: perennial root crops, bulbs, and rhizomes that produce a harvest below the soil surface. The root layer makes productive use of space that otherwise contributes nothing above ground. It is one of the seven layers used to describe and design forest gardens.

content.text: makes productive use of ground under the canopy where fruiting crops cannot grow. Root crops do not need full sun to ripen: they convert light into root mass underground and can tolerate the part-shade conditions in a young to mid-aged forest garden.
Best species for the root layer

Jerusalem artichoke is the most productive: it tolerates shade, grows tall (providing a windbreak), and produces reliably each year. Skirret produces a smaller crop in shade and is easier to manage in a confined space. Oca needs more light and suits the sunny edges rather than under a dense canopy.

Plant root crops in the gaps between trees and shrubs where the soil is accessible. Avoid planting directly under a dense canopy where surface roots from established trees compete actively. The best position is at the dripline of the tree, where the soil is enriched by leaf litter and some light reaches the ground.

Dig root crops carefully with a fork, working from the outside in to avoid hitting tree roots. Annual digging in the same spot tends to cut some tree feeder roots: this is not usually harmful if the tree is established. For Jerusalem artichoke, leave a few tubers in the ground after harvest rather than attempting to lift every one.
